viewing_check: Photos are 800 x 600 and soft: confirm the pencil signature and date lower right (looks like 'Dyer 81'), look on the back for a gallery label or the 'Still Water Study' title, check the paper for foxing, cockling and mat burn, and confirm it is an original (raised gouache, drips) rather than a print. Check whether 31 x 39 cm is the image or the sheet; comparables give image size. The nearest dated outside sale is Riverbank, 36 x 40 cm, A$1,500 at Lawsons on 28 Oct 2026; a 40 x 36 cm Dyer abstract on paper got no bids at A$700 at Leonard Joel in Jul 2026; Dyer works on paper of 55 x 75 cm sold for A$800 to A$2,100 in 2025-26, and two 30 x 40 cm estate oils made A$1,000 and A$1,200. Several known entries were misread on the earlier pass and are corrected above (Valley Landscape passed, Riverbend A$1,400, Tasmanian Landscape A$1,600, Iron Ore Creek sold A$3,000, Davidson 1 Jun 2026 figures).

identification: Large portrait-format abstract coastal landscape attributed to Ryllton Viney: ochre horizon over a black sea band and cream cliff forms, brushed aluminium frame. Back label handwritten 'RYLLTON VINEY / "DARK SEA - LIGHT CLIFFS." / 2003.' on a brown board backing, with a large handwritten mark beside it. No signature visible on the front in the online photos (both lower corners checked).

entries.note: 'A Quiet Moment of Surrender', Ryllton Viney, acrylic and sand on canvas, a current work. This page and the gallery's other Viney listings (To Rearrange is to Redefine I and II 120 x 100, The Legacy of Empire 152 x 92, Before the Light Fades 100 x 100, In the Eye of the Storm 92 x 76, The Road We Travel 152 x 92, The Silence of Winter I 137 x 121) show no price online, so the known A$2,500 snippet could not be confirmed.

viewing_check: No auction or eBay sale of a Ryllton Viney work was found outside the local rooms, so nothing outside them can set a maximum. Check the front for a signature (none seen in the photos), whether the support is board or canvas, whether it is really oil (his current gallery works are mostly acrylic with sand and charcoal), whether the fine lines in the cream area are drawn or are paint cracking, and the back label, which is the only attribution seen.
